chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from al-Hasan ibn al-Hasan, and Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, and Hasan ibn Ali, and Muhsin ibn Ali ibn Yusuf, all from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Hammad ibn Talhah, the companion of al-Sabiri, from Mu'adh ibn Kathir, the seller of garments, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

It is made easy for our Shias to spend from what is in their hands in a good manner. So when our Qa'im (Riser) rises, peace be upon him, it becomes forbidden for every owner of a hoard to keep his hoard, until they bring it to him so that he may make use of it.

As for the conquered lands, every land whose people have been established to have surrendered it to us, it is valid for us to transact in it by purchasing from them, and by exchange, and whatever follows their manner.

As for the lands of the khraj (land tax), and the lands of the anfal (spoils/public property), and those from which their people have cleared out, we have also been permitted to transact in them as long as the Imam (peace be upon him) is in concealment. So when he appears, he will see fit in that matter as he sees fit, and we will be in our transactions without sin.
And we have previously presented what indicates that, and what indicates it also is what he narrated.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on land ownership and transactions during the occultation of the Imam?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the jurisprudential basis for private property ownership during the Imam's Occultation, distinguishing between lands with established ownership and those classified as *khraj* or *anfal*. It clarifies that while the Imam retains ultimate authority to determine the fate of these lands upon his reappearance, the Shia are permitted to engage in buying, selling, and other transactions without sin during the period of concealment. This ruling underscores the practical autonomy of the community in economic affairs while maintaining the Imam's supreme jurisdiction.
